newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Solana launches new era in NATO-Ukraine relations.
newsitem.headline: Solana launches new era in NATO-Ukraine relations.

text.p: NATO Secretary General Javier Solana, fresh from inconclusive talks on a new post-Cold War partnership with Moscow, launched a new era in relations with Russia's neighbour Ukraine on Wednesday.

"I had the opportunity this morning to hand to President (Leonid) Kuchma the first draft of our document that eventually will be the NATO-Ukraine bilateral relationship," Solana told reporters after meeting the former Soviet republic's leader.
"I'm sure we will be able to work fast enough so that we can formally sign the document on the occasion of the summit that will take place in Madrid on July 8 and 9."

As warm words were exchanged in Kiev, which wants its own special relationship with NATO, Russia was demanding further compromise from the Western defence alliance before signing an accord to define their post-Cold War relations.
But Solana said progress had been made in the latest round of talks with Russia on Tuesday and that he hoped the new deal with Moscow would be signed on the target date of May 27.
Ukraine does not share Russia's opposition to NATO plans to admit Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic at the July summit.
But like Russia, it wants something on paper to fend off any security threat as Europe restructures its defence lines despite lingering suspicions of the Soviet Union's old enemy.

Ukraine is split between supporters of independence who look to the West for backing against any future threat from Moscow and ethnic Russians nostalgic for the Soviet past who would like to see Kremlin control restored in Ukraine.

Nationalists held up pro-NATO banners as Solana praised Ukraine's active role in the alliance's Partnership for Peace programme and its contribution of 500 troops to keeping the peace in Bosnia and Slovenia.
"Eastern border of NATO - eastern border of Ukraine," one banner read, showing support for Ukraine's future membership of the alliance as Solana addressed reporters and diplomats.
Hundreds of students cheered Solana as he opened an information centre which he said he hoped would give Ukrainians a better idea of their country's cooperation with NATO.
Foreign Minister Hennady Udovenko said he wanted it to dispel "myths" believed by some of the population of 51 million that the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation was an aggressor.
Ukraine is not seeking membership of the alliance for now but wants a consultation mechanism to be set up which addresses security problems as Europe redraws its defence lines.
Solana and Kuchma both described their meetings as fruitful. Western diplomats said Ukraine had promised to ratify a flank agreement putting limits on military forces in Europe by May 15.

Failure by signatories of the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty to ratify the flank agreement could hold up the process of modernising the CFE to fit the post-Cold War era -- part of the West's effort to pave the way for NATO enlargement.

Ukraine, Moldova, Georgia and Azerbaijan have been reluctant to go along with the changes, which followed Russian complaints that constraints on deploying conventional weapons restricted its ability to meet security requirements in the north Caucasus.
Ground forces attached to Russia's lion's share of the former Soviet Black Sea Fleet -- based on Ukraine's Crimean peninsula -- were included in the negotiations.
Relations between Russia and Ukraine have been under strain since Kiev won independence in 1991 because of differences over how to divide the fleet and where to base it.
